Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Politician
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Vignette:
Arthur is a man accustomed to control. At sixty-eight, his political career has been built on a foundation of steady confidence and the ability to command a room with a well-reasoned argument. That foundation shattered six months ago on a wet Tuesday night. Driving home from a late-session dinner, a pair of headlights had swerved violently into his lane. The memory of the event does not exist for him as a coherent narrative, but as a series of blindingly clear, still images. He remembers the sudden, brilliant glare of the other car’s lights, a snapshot of the driver’s face—slack and surprised—and then the crystalline spiderweb of his own windshield just before impact. When he tries to explain what happened, even to his wife, the words tangle and fail him; he loses the thread, trailing off into a frustrated silence as the images flood his mind. With them comes a phantom echo of the initial, searing pain in his ribs and shoulder, a physical ghost of the impact that makes him flinch in the present.

In the weeks that followed the accident, Arthur’s world began to shrink. He stopped driving entirely. The simple act of getting behind the wheel, or even sitting in the passenger seat, became unbearable. His wife now drives him everywhere, a concession that feels to Arthur like a daily admission of failure. His work, once a source of pride, has become a minefield. During a recent fundraising gala, a donor leaned in to speak with him, and the faint smell of whiskey on the man’s breath—the same smell that had clung to the other driver—sent a jolt of ice through his veins. He froze mid-sentence, his mind blank, able to think only of the need to get away. He feels constantly exposed, certain that his colleagues and constituents can see the damage in him just by looking at his face, as if the trauma were a visible brand on his skin. This belief has become a certainty for him: the accident was not random. It happened, he has come to believe, because of a fundamental flaw in his character, a carelessness he has spent a lifetime trying to conceal.

This self-blame is a constant, churning internal monologue. He spends hours in his study, not reading the legislative briefs that pile up, but replaying the seconds before the crash, convinced he could have done something different. The thoughts circle endlessly: he should have taken the other route, he should have reacted faster, he was complacent. His concentration is shattered; he will read the same paragraph five times without comprehension, the words blurring into meaninglessness. The quiet of his home office, once a sanctuary for thought, now feels menacing. An unusual silence makes him feel as though something terrible is about to happen, the calm before an inevitable storm. He must be on guard at all times, scanning every room, every face, for a threat he cannot name.

Sleep offers no escape. Arthur finds himself waking several times a night, heart pounding, with a desperate need to check that the doors are locked and his wife is safe beside him. Any feeling of physical discomfort—a slight indigestion, a muscle ache—can spiral into a sense of imminent danger, his body’s signals reinterpreted as warnings. He feels trapped in a state of high alert that is utterly exhausting. The final impetus for seeking help came last week, during a televised town hall. An image of a roadside accident flashed on a screen behind a reporter, and Arthur felt the room tilt. The snapshot of the crumpled cars triggered his own fragmented memories so powerfully that he lost his place completely, standing mute at the podium for what felt like an eternity. It was the public display of his private ruin that made him realize he could no longer manage this alone. He has come to therapy not with a clear goal, but with a desperate, quiet hope of silencing the internal critic and finding his way back to the man who believed he was in control of his own life.
